State Minister for Health and Family Welfare Dr MA Muhit told the third session of parliament that the government expected the cancer, kidney and cardiac hospitals under construction in eight divisional cities to become fully operational by the next fiscal year.
“Given the alarming cancer situation in the country, the disease is being given special priority,” he said.
However, increasing the number of hospital beds alone will not be enough to ease patients' suffering. Addressing staff shortages, inadequate medicine supplies and complications in the admission process is also essential.
Otherwise, relatives fear, patients seeking treatment will continue to face the indignity of spending nights outside hospital gates because they cannot secure admission.

item.title: President calls for stronger Bangladesh-China ties
item.description:
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on Wednesday called for further strengthening bilateral relations between Bangladesh and China, describing the country as a trusted friend and an important strategic partner.
He made the remarks when Minister of the International Department of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee Liu Haixing paid a courtesy call on him at Bangabhaban, President's Press Secretary Md Sarwar Alam told UNB.
During the meeting, the president referred to the signing of a framework agreement for the modernisation and expansion of Mongla Port and the groundbreaking of the Chinese Economic and Industrial Zone (CEIZ), saying these initiatives would make significant contributions to Bangladesh's connectivity, industrialisation and economic development.
He also welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping's proposals for expanding multidimensional connectivity, including the proposed Kunming-Chittagong corridor and the China-Myanmar-Bangladesh Economic Corridor.
Mirza Fakhrul thanked and congratulated Xi Jinping and invited him to visit Bangladesh at a convenient time.
Emphasising greater Chinese investment in Bangladesh, he highlighted sectors that could contribute to technology transfer, employment generation and export diversification.
Liu Haixing assured continued Chinese cooperation in areas such as green energy, education and cultural exchanges.
The president thanked China for its support in financing and constructing the 1,000-bed Bangladesh-China Friendship General Hospital and sought Beijing's continued active role in ensuring the safe repatriation of Rohingyas to Myanmar.
The Chinese minister assured that China would continue its cooperation in this regard.
Mirza Fakhrul also expressed gratitude for China's continued assistance amid the ongoing energy crisis.
Recalling the visits to China by Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman in 1977 and 1980, he said those historic visits had laid the foundation for bilateral relations between the two countries.
Liu Haixing said Bangladesh's diplomatic relations with China had been established during Ziaur Rahman's tenure and further strengthened during the tenure of then prime minister Khaleda Zia.
He expressed hope that bilateral relations would become stronger and broader under the leadership of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.
Referring to his recent visit to China, the president said his meetings with the Chinese vice president and the visiting minister had been fruitful and helped further strengthen mutual relations.
Mentioning Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's visit to China in June, he said the visit would play an important role in taking bilateral relations to new heights.
Mirza Fakhrul described the prime minister's interactions with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Premier Li Qiang and other top Chinese leaders, along with the signing of memorandums of understanding and other cooperation documents, as positive developments in bilateral ties.
He wished Liu Haixing continued success and good health.
Earlier, the president welcomed the Chinese minister with flowers when he arrived at Bangabhaban and introduced him to his secretaries.
Among the members of the Chinese delegation were Chargé d'Affaires of the Chinese Embassy in Dhaka Liu Yuin and Director General of the Bureau of Southeast and South Asian Affairs of the CPC Central Committee's International Department Peng Xiubin.
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam and Foreign Ministry Secretary Salahuddin Noman Chowdhury were also present.
After the meeting, the president accompanied the Chinese minister and other delegation members on a tour of Bangabhaban.
During the visit, video footage of Liu Haixing's father, former ambassador Liu Shuqing, presenting his credentials to then President Ziaur Rahman in 1980 was shown.
Photographs of Mirza Fakhrul's visit to China during his tenure as Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives (LGRD) Minister were also displayed.
The president's military secretary, secretary of the public division and press secretary were present.

item.title: Ameer-e-Jamaat urges quick resolution of garment workers' wage dispute
item.description:
Jamaat-e-Islami Ameer Shafiqur Rahman on Wednesday urged the government to take immediate steps to resolve the ongoing garment workers' wage dispute, warning that delays would further increase losses in the country's major export sector.
In a video message, he said garment workers had been protesting in different industrial areas for the past several days demanding higher wages and other benefits, while many factories had been shut amid the unrest.
He said the rising cost of living had made it increasingly difficult for low-paid workers to make ends meet, stressing the need to revise the wage structure through discussions with both workers and factory owners.
“An industry can survive only if its workers survive,” he said, urging the government to fulfil its responsibilities without further delay to prevent additional losses and avoid creating opportunities for further instability.
The Jamaat chief also condemned the killing of Taufiq, a garment worker from Gaibandha, in Sreepur of Gazipur, and demanded a fair investigation to bring those responsible to justice as soon as possible.
He said the garment sector was the country's principal export industry and that any major disruption in the sector could severely affect the national economy.
He also cautioned that opportunists might try to exploit the situation, calling on the government and all concerned to act responsibly and remain vigilant.
Urging workers to protect their workplaces, the Jamaat chief said he stood by their legitimate demands and called on factory owners to treat workers as members of their own families.
He said cooperation between workers and owners would make it easier to reach a solution, while prolonged indecision would only worsen the situation.
He called on the government to act quickly to resolve the dispute, prevent further damage to the industry and ensure that workers received their rightful wages.

item.title: Arrest warrant issued against Pori Moni
item.description:
A Dhaka court has issued arrest warrants against actor Pori Moni and her costume designer, Junaid Bogdadi Jimmy, in a case filed over allegations of assault, vandalism and intimidation.
Dhaka Senior Judicial Magistrate Mahfuzur Rahman passed the order on Wednesday afternoon after a hearing.
Alamgir, bench assistant of the court, confirmed the development, saying the court rejected a time petition filed by the defence and cancelled the accused's bail. The court also set December 23 for recording witness statements.
The plaintiff appeared before the court on Wednesday and sought cancellation of the accused's bail. No defence lawyer was present during the hearing.
On March 18, 2024, investigation officer Inspector Md Monir Hossain of the Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI), Dhaka district, submitted a report to the Dhaka Chief Judicial Magistrate's Court, finding the allegations of assault and intimidation against Pori Moni and her costume designer, Junaid Bogdadi Jimmy, also known as Jim, to be true.
However, the investigation found no evidence against another accused, Fatema Tuz Jannat Boni.
On January 26 last year, the court framed charges in the case and ordered the trial to begin.
Nasir Uddin filed the case with a Dhaka court on July 6, 2022.
According to the case statement, Pori Moni and her associates allegedly entered various high-end clubs, consumed alcohol and took away parcels without paying.
The statement also alleged that Pori Moni threatened to harass the plaintiff by filing false cases through police officers known to her.
It said that shortly after midnight on June 9, 2021, the accused entered Savar Boat Club and used a washroom on the second floor before sitting inside the club and consuming alcohol.
At around 1:15am, as the plaintiff and his associate Shah Shahidul Alam were leaving the club, Pori Moni allegedly called Nasir Uddin and asked him to sit with them for a while.
She allegedly made obscene gestures towards him and pressured him to provide a bottle of Blue Label alcohol free of charge.
When he refused, Pori Moni allegedly abused him verbally. During an argument, she allegedly threw a serving glass and her mobile phone at him, injuring his head and chest.
The case statement further alleged that Pori Moni and her associates assaulted Nasir Uddin, vandalised property and threatened to kill him.
Following the incident, Pori Moni filed a case with Savar police station against Nasir Uddin and another person, accusing them of attempted rape and attempted murder.
The case is currently pending before Dhaka Women and Children Repression Prevention Tribunal-9.

item.title: 55 years on, 15 Thanchi villages still await a bridge
item.description:
More than 1,000 people from 15 remote villages in Thanchi upazila of Bandarban have been risking their lives crossing a rocky stream due to the absence of a permanent bridge in the Padmamukh area of Tindu union.
Residents of two mouzas, belonging to the Marma, Tripura and Mro communities, have to cross a nearly 400-foot-long stretch of Padma Jhir using makeshift bamboo bridges, which they build themselves every year.
The lack of a permanent bridge has caused prolonged hardship, disrupting access to education and healthcare and making it difficult to transport agricultural produce and other essential goods.
Despite 55 years of independence, the remote hill communities remain deprived of basic infrastructure, locals said. The situation becomes particularly dangerous during the monsoon, when rising water levels and strong currents often leave the villages virtually cut off.
Local Union Parishad member Uhlamong Marma said Padma Jhiri is about 15km from Thanchi upazila headquarters.
“Many tourists also use this risky route, but no measures have been taken to ensure safe passage,” he said.
A recent visit to the area found no permanent bridge or safe crossing facility over the stream. Villagers have been relying on the same route for generations, facing an increased risk of accidents during the rainy season.
Local residents Uziram Tripura and Khubaiti Tripura said they had to build bamboo bridges every year using their own resources.
They said the lack of a permanent bridge puts children, elderly people and patients at particular risk, while hampering education, healthcare and the transportation of agricultural produce.
Tindu Union Parishad Chairman Bhagya Chandra Tripura said the union council lacked the funds to construct a durable bridge.
He called on the upazila administration and relevant authorities to take urgent steps to ease residents' suffering by constructing a permanent bridge over Padma Jhiri.
Thanchi Upazila Executive Engineer of the Local Government Engineering Department (LGED), Md Abu Saleh Hanif, said the crossing was extremely important for local residents.
He said residents had been asked to submit an application so that the authorities could consider the project.
“If necessary, we will visit the site and try to include the project in a future budget for implementation,” he added.

item.title: Bangladesh, Kosovo stress parliamentary ties, trade and investment
item.description:
National Parliament Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad Bir Bikram on Wednesday held a courtesy meeting with Kosovo Ambassador to Bangladesh Lulzim Plana at his office in the Parliament Complex, highlighting the need to strengthen parliamentary cooperation, trade and investment between the two countries.
During the meeting, the speaker said the people of Kosovo had made supreme sacrifices for their country's independence, adding that Bangladesh and Kosovo shared common bonds of independence and cultural heritage.
He also highlighted the close cultural ties between the two nations, said a press release issued by the Parliament Secretariat this evening.
The speaker alleged that the democratic rights of the people of Bangladesh had been undermined over the past 17 years through farcical elections.
He said the Awami League government had established a reign of terror through enforced disappearances, killings, extrajudicial executions and vote rigging.
Referring to the UN fact-finding report, the Speaker said it had exposed the brutal and inhumane nature of the previous government's rule.
He said the July Mass Uprising of 2024 had ended Sheikh Hasina's autocratic rule and paved the way for Bangladesh's renewed democratic journey.
Major Hafiz described the 13th parliamentary election as one of the freest, fairest and most credible elections in the country's history. He said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman was working to fulfill the aspirations of the people.
Kosovo Ambassador Lulzim Plana said a new democratic chapter had begun in Bangladesh, praising the active participation of lawmakers in parliamentary debates.
He noted that a large section of Bangladesh's population was young and economically active, saying they could make significant contributions to the national economy through quality education and information technology (IT) skills.
The ambassador expressed gratitude to Bangladesh for recognising Kosovo as an independent state and invited the Speaker to visit Kosovo.
Both sides emphasised the formation of a parliamentary caucus between the two countries, expansion of trade and investment, promotion of joint academic and research activities, and strengthening of exchanges in sports and culture.
Representatives of the Kosovo Embassy, the Parliament Secretariat secretary and other senior officials concerned were present at the meeting.

item.title: Experts: Chittagong’s RMG renewable energy transition needs tailored solutions
item.description:
Leaders across Bangladesh’s garment and textile sector called for stronger policy implementation, accessible green financing, and shared supply-chain responsibility to turn decarbonization commitments into reality.
The consensus emerged at a multistakeholder dialogue titled "Promoting Sustainable Apparel and Textile Industry in Bangladesh through Decarbonization and Renewable Energy Transition: Policy and Implementation Priorities," organized by Ethical Trading Initiative (ETI) Bangladesh at Hotel Agrabad in Chittagong on Wednesday.
The event convened 40 stakeholders representing the BGMEA, BKMEA, trade union federations, financial institutions, global brands, NGOs, and civil society to address the challenges of accelerating renewable energy adoption within Chittagong’s specific industrial landscape while safeguarding workers.
Participants stressed that setting target numbers alone will not ensure implementation without clear approval procedures, financing, technical support, and stable business relationships to counter rising production costs and energy supply instability.
Highlighting local industrial realities, Md M Mohiuddin Chowdhury, director of BGMEA and CEO/director of Clifton Group, pointed out that unreliable electricity and voltage fluctuations continue to jeopardize machinery, output, and market competitiveness.
Echoing operational hurdles, Md Yasin, director of BKMEA and managing director of Sonnet Group of Companies Ltd., urged regulators to simplify net-metering procedures, grant tax concessions on solar equipment, and unlock affordable green financing.
Addressing supply-chain economics, Md Ismail Murad, corporate responsibility manager at Columbia Sportswear Company, stressed that manufacturers operating on narrow margins cannot shoulder the full financial weight of decarbonization targets alone.
Robiul Hoque Shimul, organizing secretary of the Bangladesh Labour Federation, along with other labour leaders, called for structured employer-worker dialogue to protect employment, guarantee fair wages, maintain safe working conditions, and ensure equitable reskilling as automation accelerates—particularly for women workers.
From the financial sector, Saiful A Chowdhury, area head for Chittagong at Brac Bank PLC, outlined available green financing options under Bangladesh Bank’s refinancing schemes, calling for greater awareness and a shift in mindset among manufacturers to leverage these tools.
Abil Bin Amin, executive director of ETI Bangladesh, reaffirmed that energy efficiency and renewable energy investment must advance together.
"Fair prices, long-term partnerships, and enabling policies are essential to making this transition workable for factories and workers," he stated.
Key recommendations
To accelerate the transition, delegates urged government authorities and regulators to streamline approval processes for renewable installations, particularly by simplifying net-metering and grid-connection procedures in CEPZ and KEPZ.
Alongside these administrative fixes, financial institutions must expand access to affordable green finance by easing collateral requirements and providing clear guidance for smaller, less-resourced factories.
Additionally, policy frameworks must account for enterprises in shared buildings through offsite generation models and collective energy procurement, while encouraging factories to integrate renewable investments with broader resource efficiency measures like energy audits, heat recovery, and water conservation.
Crucially, the dialogue emphasized that successful implementation hinges on a just, shared commitment across the entire supply chain and workforce.
Global brands were called on to co-fund these sustainability goals through fair pricing, predictable order volumes, and longer-term sourcing agreements rather than leaving factory owners to bear the full burden.
Concurrently, labour representatives stressed that worker rights, safe conditions, fair wages, and inclusive upskilling programs—especially for women—must remain central to all transition planning to ensure that greening the industry delivers tangible social benefits.

item.title: SBAC Bank holds training on OEMS and FDI reporting
item.description:
SBAC Bank PLC.’s Learning & Development Center recently organized a daylong training workshop on ‘Reporting of Online Export Monitoring System (OEMS) & Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)’.
Md Rashed Akter, SEVP & head of retail distribution division of SBAC Bank PLC, inaugurated the workshop.
The resource persons were Md Hassan Shahriar, additional director, Foreign Exchange Investment Department, Bangladesh Bank, and Shahjahan Kabir, vice president, ICMITS, Mutual Trust Bank PLC.
Md Saidur Rahman, principal of the Learning & Development Center, and Md Mazharul Hasan, SVP & head of international division of SBAC Bank PLC., were also present.
The workshop focused on accurate export reporting through OEMS and FDI reporting to Bangladesh Bank.
A total of 62 participants attended the training program.

item.title: Bank Asia reports 34% growth in net profit in first nine months of 2026
item.description:
Bank Asia’s net profit for the first nine months of 2026 increased by 34% compared to the same period of last year.
From January to September 2026, the bank recorded a net profit of Tk472 crore, which was Tk351 crore during the same period in 2025.
To disclose the profit to shareholders, Bank Asia PLC. organized an online based Earnings Disclosure Q3-2026 on November 3, 2026 at Bank Asia Tower, Karwan Bazar, Dhaka.
Sohail RK Hussain, managing director of the bank, along with additional managing directors, deputy managing directors, chief financial officer, and head of audit were present at the program.
According to the bank, the NPL ratio has declined significantly, while deposits increased by 19%, rising from Tk44,615 crore to Tk53,308 crore, boosting operating profit.
As of end of September 2026, the bank’s earnings per share (EPS) stood at Tk3.24 marking a 37% growth, compared to Tk2.37 a year earlier. Its net asset value (NAV) per share reached Tk28.46 marking a 5% increase year-on-year.
During the July–September quarter, the bank posted a net profit of approximately Tk208 crore.
The bank also reported significant increase in its operating cash flow supported primarily by substantial growth in customer deposits.

item.title: DRU expresses concern over journalist Rajib Ghosh being taken to DB office
item.description:
The Dhaka Reporters Unity (DRU) has expressed deep concern over its permanent member and DBC News Special Correspondent Rajib Ghosh being taken to the Detective Branch (DB) office.
In a statement issued on Wednesday, DRU President Abu Saleh Akon and General Secretary Mynul Hasan Sohel raised concerns on behalf of the organisation's executive committee.
They said the incident had caused concern among journalists and stressed that any action by law enforcement agencies must follow existing laws and due legal process.
The DRU leaders said any allegations against a journalist should be addressed through established legal procedures. They also stressed the need for transparency and accountability to protect press freedom and journalists' professional rights.
They demanded that Rajib's whereabouts be immediately disclosed to his family and colleagues and that he be released promptly if there is no legal basis for holding him.

item.title: PM’s Mongla visit raises hopes for economic growth in southwest
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is scheduled to visit Mongla Port and Khulna on Thursday, raising expectations of a major boost to port capacity, investment, and employment across the southwestern region.
During the visit, he will lay the foundation stone for a Tk4,068 crore project to construct two container jetties and develop associated facilities at Mongla Port.
The port project is expected to modernize infrastructure, increase cargo-handling capacity, and create new opportunities for domestic and foreign investment, generating employment in the region.
According to Mongla Port Authority, the project follows an agreement signed between Bangladesh and China on October 10. China will provide Tk3,593 crore, while the Bangladesh government will contribute Tk475 crore.
The project includes a 368-metre container terminal and yard, specialized facilities for handling hazardous goods, and 49 pieces of equipment. Once completed, the facilities will enable the port to handle more than 30 containers per hour and raise its annual handling capacity to 400,000 TEUs.
The prime minister will also attend the signing of a memorandum of understanding between Invent Bangladesh and China Railway Construction Corporation (CRCC).
State Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change Sheikh Faridul Islam said the visit would help establish Mongla Port as an important hub for international trade while accelerating economic activities, and creating employment opportunities across the region.
After visiting Mongla, the prime minister will pay his respects at the shrine of Hazrat Khan Jahan Ali before travelling to Khulna District Stadium to inaugurate the "Notun Kuri sports competition (season 2)".
At a press briefing, National Parliament Whip Rakibul Islam said the initiative would encourage young people to pursue sports professionally and help restore Khulna's reputation as a sports city.
Youth and Sports Ministry Secretary Mahfuzul Alam Khan said around 16.23 lakh online registrations had been received for the sports competition, compared with 168,000 in the first. The competition will feature 10 sporting events.

item.title: Moyeen Khan returns home from hospital
item.description:
Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives Minister and BNP Standing Committee Member Dr Abdul Moyeen Khan returned home from hospital on Wednesday afternoon after receiving treatment.
He was discharged from Evercare Hospital Dhaka at 3:30pm, said BNP Media Cell Member Sayrul Kabir Khan.
Moyeen Khan was admitted to the hospital on October 21 after suddenly falling ill.
He received treatment under the supervision of a medical board.
According to doctors' advice, he will have to take rest for a few more days.

item.title: COP31: Another promise to the planet?
item.description:
The longer the list of promises to save our planet grows, the faster the window of opportunity to address the climate crisis appears to be closing.
For more than three decades, world leaders have gathered at international climate conferences, announcing ambitious targets, establishing financial mechanisms, and pledging to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
Yet rising global temperatures, extreme weather events, sea-level rise, and climate-related losses and damages have become increasingly alarming realities.
This persistent contradiction raises a fundamental question: Are new commitments truly driving meaningful change, or is each successive conference simply adding another layer of promises to those that remain unfulfilled?
The 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) is scheduled to take place from November 9 to 20, 2026, in Antalya, Türkiye. Türkiye will preside over the conference, while Australia will lead the formal negotiations.
The particular significance of this year's conference lies in its stated emphasis on implementing previous decisions alongside pursuing new commitments. However, understanding whether these expectations are realistic requires examining the historical evolution of international climate diplomacy.
1992-2015: From Rio to Paris, the historic journey of climate commitments
The institutional foundation of international climate cooperation was established through the adoption of the UNFCCC at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit. Its underlying principle recognized that climate change is a global challenge, but countries differ in their historical responsibilities and capacities to address it.
The first Conference of the Parties, held in 1995, initiated a process of regular international climate negotiations. The Kyoto Protocol, adopted in 1997, established legally binding emissions-reduction targets for developed countries covered by its commitments. Although an important milestone, limited participation and implementation challenges constrained its effectiveness in controlling global emissions.
At the 2009 Copenhagen conference, developed countries committed to mobilizing $100 billion annually by 2020 to support climate action in developing countries. However, the target was not achieved within the agreed timeframe.
According to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), climate finance reached $115.9 billion in 2022, exceeding the annual target for the first time, two years after the agreed deadline. This delay further exposed the crisis of confidence between developed and developing countries in international climate negotiations.
The Paris Agreement, adopted in 2015, marked a historic turning point in climate diplomacy. Countries agreed to hold the increase in global average temperature well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels while pursuing efforts to limit warming to 1.5°C. They also committed to submitting increasingly ambitious Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) every five years.
2021-2023: A new chapter in climate justice and energy transition
At COP26 in Glasgow in 2021, countries collectively called for the phasedown of unabated coal power and the phaseout of inefficient fossil-fuel subsidies for the first time in a COP decision. The conference also reaffirmed the importance of strengthening climate adaptation and financial support.
However, no binding timetable was established for a complete transition away from fossil fuels. COP27, held in Sharm El-Sheikh, Egypt, in 2022, achieved an important breakthrough. Following prolonged negotiations, countries agreed to establish a Loss and Damage Fund to support vulnerable developing nations suffering from climate-related impacts.
For Bangladesh and other climate-vulnerable countries, this represented significant recognition of climate justice and the need to address damages associated with a crisis to which they have contributed relatively little.
At COP28 in Dubai in 2023, the first Global Stocktake under the Paris Agreement was completed. The conference called for transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems in a just, orderly, and equitable manner. It also highlighted the need to triple global renewable-energy capacity and double the global average annual rate of energy-efficiency improvement by 2030.
The decision to operationalize the Loss and Damage Fund was another important achievement. Nevertheless, the absence of clear, enforceable implementation obligations and adequate financial resources remained major limitations of these decisions.
COP29: New financial commitments, persistent implementation concerns
COP29, held in Baku, Azerbaijan, in 2024, focused primarily on climate finance. After extensive negotiations, countries agreed on a new goal of mobilizing at least $300bn annually for developing countries by 2035, with developed countries taking the lead.
A broader objective of scaling climate finance from public and private sources to $1.3 trillion annually by 2035 was also advanced. Although the new financial target represented a substantial increase over the previous $100bn commitment, many developing countries considered it insufficient compared with their actual needs of climate adaptation, the transition to clean energy, and responses to climate-related losses and damages which require enormous financial investment.
Beyond the amount pledged, the nature of climate finance remains equally important. Loan-dependent assistance can increase the debt burden of climate-vulnerable countries. Therefore, grants, concessional financing, technology transfer, and accessible funding arrangements must receive greater attention.
The fundamental concern is whether these financial commitments will translate into timely and effective assistance for the countries and communities that need it most.
COP30: Familiar questions remained
COP30, held in Belém, Brazil, in November 2025, was presented as a conference focused on implementing climate commitments. Its location in the Amazon region highlighted the interconnections among forest conservation, biodiversity, and the global climate crisis.
The conference adopted the Belém Political Package. One of the key outcomes was an agreement calling for climate adaptation finance to be at least tripled by 2035, indicators for measuring progress towards the Global Goal on Adaptation, and initiatives such as the Global Implementation Accelerator and the Belém Mission to 1.5°C.
However, the collective outcome did not include a binding, time-bound roadmap for transitioning away from fossil fuels. The Brazilian COP30 presidency subsequently initiated a separate process to develop relevant roadmaps.
Consequently, despite progress in negotiations, fundamental political disagreements over emissions reductions remained largely unresolved.
More concerningly, the United Nations Environment Program's (UNEP) 2025 assessment indicated that existing policies could result in approximately 2.8°C of global warming during this century.
Even if the latest national climate commitments were fully implemented, projected warming could remain between 2.3°C and 2.5°C. These estimates demonstrate that a considerable gap continues to exist between internationally agreed temperature goals and the actions required to achieve them.
COP31: A new era of implementation?
Against this background, the most important question facing COP31 is how previous commitments can be translated into practical action.
Reducing greenhouse gas emissions requires realistic country-specific implementation schedules, transparent progress assessments, and effective accountability mechanisms.
Similarly, announcing additional climate-finance targets will not be sufficient without examining actual financial delivery.
How much of the promised finance has been disbursed? What proportion has been provided as grants rather than loans? How much has reached vulnerable communities? These questions require transparent and measurable answers.
Strong international cooperation will also be essential for implementing the latest NDCs submitted around 2025. Meaningful progress will be difficult without balancing the historical responsibilities of developed countries, the development needs of emerging economies, and the principles of global climate justice.
COP31 should therefore become an opportunity to remove barriers to implementing earlier decisions rather than another competition to announce new commitments.
Bangladesh's expectations
Bangladesh contributes a relatively small share of global greenhouse gas emissions -- approximately 0.44% in 2024 -- yet remains highly exposed to multiple climate-related hazards.
Coastal salinity, cyclones, floods, droughts, riverbank erosion, and irregular rainfall increasingly threaten agriculture, water resources, infrastructure, and livelihoods.
According to Bangladesh's NDC 3.0, submitted in 2025, the country aims to reduce its projected greenhouse gas emissions by 20.31% by 2035 relative to a business-as-usual scenario.
This includes an unconditional reduction of 6.39% through domestic efforts and an additional conditional reduction of 13.92% dependent on international support.
Achieving these targets will require increased investment in renewable energy, efficient irrigation, climate-resilient agriculture, improved waste management, and technological capacity.
At the same time, easier access to adaptation finance and the Loss and Damage Fund remains essential. Bangladesh should therefore emphasize needs-based climate financing, grant-based assistance, technology transfer, and stronger international support for locally implementable adaptation projects.
For Bangladesh, climate diplomacy must ultimately deliver practical benefits to vulnerable populations rather than remain confined to international agreements.
The world needs action, not repeated promises
It would be unjustified to describe international climate conferences as complete failures. The Paris Agreement, the establishment of the Loss and Damage Fund, renewable-energy commitments, and climate-finance frameworks represent important achievements in international cooperation.
However, their effectiveness will ultimately depend on implementation. The success of COP31 should not be judged by the length of its final declaration, the number of newly announced commitments, or the financial figures presented at the negotiating table.
Instead, it should be measured by actual reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, climate finance reaching vulnerable communities, and demonstrable improvements in climate resilience.
The world does not need another layer of climate commitments. It needs credible evidence that existing promises are being fulfilled. Whether COP31 can initiate that transformation remains one of the most important questions facing global climate diplomacy.
Dr Md Shahjahan Kabir is Former Director General, BRRI.

item.title: An eye on food security
item.description:
The Bangladesh Rice Research Institute's (BRRI) development of BRRI Dhan 119, a high-yielding, salt-tolerant rice variety, is a welcome achievement that deserves recognition and continued support.
With an average yield of 5.7 tons per hectare, and the potential to produce up to 7.6 tons under favourable conditions, the new variety offers considerable promise for farmers in coastal regions. It can tolerate significant levels of soil salinity, making it particularly valuable in areas where rising salinity has long restricted agricultural production.
Additionally, its shorter growing period of approximately 115 days has the potential to create opportunities to cultivate additional winter crops, including sunflower and salt-tolerant mustard, allowing farmers to make better use of their land.
This is particularly important as climate change continues to threaten Bangladesh's agricultural landscape. Rising sea levels, saltwater intrusion, and increasingly unpredictable weather patterns are putting pressure on traditional farming practices. Hence, developing resilient crop varieties is one of the most practical ways to protect agricultural productivity and strengthen long-term food security.
However, scientific achievements must translate into tangible benefits for farmers. Ensuring an adequate supply of quality seeds, making them affordable, and providing farmers with the necessary technical guidance will be crucial. Agricultural extension services must also help farmers understand the variety's suitability for different soil conditions and cultivation practices.
Research institutions should continue monitoring field performance and improving varieties to address emerging challenges.
Equally important is sustained investment in agricultural research. Our scientists have demonstrated that local expertise can produce solutions to distinctly local problems. Their work must receive consistent funding, institutional support, and opportunities for further innovation.
Food security cannot depend on production figures alone. It requires a resilient agricultural sector that can adapt to changing conditions while protecting farmers' livelihoods.
While BRRI Dhan 119 is a positive step in that direction, the challenge now is to ensure that this achievement reaches the fields and farmers who need it most.

item.title: We need better ways to raise revenue
item.description:
The National Board of Revenue’s decision to issue door-to-door notices to non-filing TIN holders may appear to widen the tax net, but is a strategy that risks becoming administrative pressure rather than meaningful reform.
The truth of the matter is that Bangladesh cannot build a stronger revenue system merely by sending notices to every name on a database.
In fact, the numbers point to a more basic problem: Of nearly 13 million TIN holders, only around five million filed returns in the previous fiscal year. Yet the NBR does not know how many remaining accounts belong to deceased people, individuals with no taxable income, or genuine defaulters.
Nearly 40% of notices are reportedly returned because addresses are outdated, while only 10% of recipients respond. Pursuing such records without first fixing the database is unlikely to generate substantial revenue.
The priority should be to modernize tax administration. The NBR needs an integrated, regularly updated database linked with civil registration and government records. It must make TIN cancellation and return submission simpler, improve digital services, and ensure taxpayers understand their obligations without unnecessary visits to tax offices.
Enforcement should focus on deliberate evasion, undisclosed wealth, and large-scale defaulters, rather than pressuring people who do not meet the income tax threshold.
More importantly, Bangladesh needs revenue targets that reflect economic realities and the capacity of its tax machinery. The NBR has repeatedly fallen short of ambitious targets, including a Tk41,879 crore deficit in the first quarter of FY27. Setting increasingly high figures without addressing structural weaknesses only creates pressure for hurried, ineffective collection drives.
Targets must be grounded in collection trends, economic growth and administrative capacity.
Revenue generation is essential to funding public services and development, but it requires public trust, fair enforcement, and a system that makes compliance easier.
The government must therefore pursue those reforms instead of relying on the current door-to-door notice system to compensate for unrealistic expectations.

item.title: Understanding the modern Bangladeshi
item.description:
Many Bangladeshis today can simultaneously feel deeply Muslim, strongly Bengali, and proudly Bangladeshi. Those identities are no longer necessarily perceived as mutually exclusive.
This synthesis did not happen overnight. It is the product of a century of political evolution, from the Muslim League to the Language Movement to the Liberation War, and a constitutional experiment that tried to codify it.
Bengali Muslim political thought was never identical to the North Indian Muslim League tradition. The two represented different answers to the same question: How should Muslims organize politically in colonial India?
In North India, from Sir Syed Ahmed Khan in the late 19th century to the All-India Muslim League founded in 1906, the emphasis was on Muslims as a minority needing educational modernization, constitutional safeguards, and eventually, recognition as a separate political nation. This trajectory culminated in the Lahore Resolution of 1940 and the creation of Pakistan in 1947.
In Bengal, there was a powerful alternative basis of identity: Bengali language, Bengali culture, and a territorial homeland. The political careers of A K Fazlul Huq, the Krishak Praja Party, and later the United Front illustrated this tendency. For the Bengali Muslim peasant, identity was simultaneously religious, linguistic, and territorial.
Thus, Bengali Muslim experience contained two competing concepts of identity: Muslim identity versus Bengali linguistic-cultural identity. After 1947, that tension became increasingly pronounced.
Pakistan’s attempt to impose Urdu as the sole state language produced the Language Movement of 1952. That movement was enormously important for the eventual development of Bangladeshi nationalism.
The Bengali Language Movement did something politically profound. It shifted the basis of collective identity from “we are Muslims living in Pakistan” toward “we are Bengalis whose language and culture constitute our collective identity.”
This did not eliminate Islam from Bengali identity. Rather, it separated religious identity from national-political identity. Religion remained central to personal and cultural life; language and culture became the basis of political nationality. That distinction eventually became fundamental to Bangladesh.
By the late 1960s and early 1970s, the Awami League’s political program under Sheikh Mujibur Rahman increasingly emphasized four principles: Bengali nationalism, democracy, economic justice (socialism), and secularism. The 1971 independence struggle transformed these from political slogans into the ideological foundations of a new state.
The Constitution of Bangladesh was adopted on November 4, 1972. Its preamble explicitly identified nationalism, socialism, democracy, and secularism as the fundamental principles of the Constitution. Article 8 made those four principles the fundamental principles of state policy.
But Article 12 gives us the most revealing definition of what the framers meant by secularism. It stated that secularism would be realized through elimination of:
That is extraordinarily significant. Bangladesh’s constitutional secularism was not primarily an attack on religion. It was principally an attack on using religion as the basis of political power and citizenship.
This is considerably closer to Indian-style constitutional secularism than to the more aggressively anti-clerical French model of laïcité.
The 1972 Constitution did not conceive secularism as “making Bangladesh a country without Muslims or without Islam.” Bangladesh was overwhelmingly Muslim from its birth.
Rather, the constitutional idea was that being Muslim, Hindu, Buddhist, or Christian should not determine one’s political status as a Bangladeshi. That is why the original Article 12 simultaneously dealt with secularism and freedom of religion.
The conceptual vocabulary of secularism certainly came through the global modern political world, ultimately influenced by European Enlightenment thought, constitutionalism, and the American and French experiences. But the political reason Bangladesh adopted secularism was overwhelmingly indigenous.
It emerged from a specific Bengali experience: Muslim League politics → Pakistan → linguistic conflict → Bengali nationalism → 1971 Liberation War → 1972 Constitution.
And Article 12 tells us what the framers were trying to prevent: Religious communalism becoming the basis of political power.
There is one particularly interesting irony. The partition that created East Pakistan was supposed to solve the Hindu-Muslim political problem by separating the two communities geographically. But East Pakistan eventually demonstrated that Muslim identity alone was insufficient to overcome linguistic, cultural, and regional identity.
For many Bengali Muslims, 1947 created Pakistan, but 1971 created a political state in which being Bengali and being Muslim no longer had to be competing identities.
That makes it possible for a Bangladeshi Muslim today to look back at undivided Bengal and say: “I am glad Bangladesh exists, but I also feel that something precious was lost when Bengal was divided.”
That sentiment is not necessarily a rejection of Pakistan’s creation by their ancestors. It is often the result of seven decades of historical experience after Pakistan. Nostalgia for pre-1947 Bengal can coexist perfectly well with the creation of Bangladesh.
There is a fascinating demographic dimension to this. The enormous Hindu exodus from East Bengal and the much smaller but still substantial Muslim movement in the opposite direction fundamentally changed the social composition of both West Bengal and East Bengal.
The memories of those two migrations are very different -- and that helps explain why nostalgia for “undivided Bengal” is expressed differently by Bengali Hindus and Bengali Muslims.
For many West Bengali Hindus, undivided Bengal is a memory of a lost ancestral home. For many Bangladeshi Muslims, it is a cultural memory -- Tagore and Nazrul, Pahela Baishakh, bhatiali songs, traditional Bengali food -- without any desire to undo 1971.
Bangladesh’s experience after 1975 complicated the picture. The initial secular-nationalist period gave way to a gradual revival of Islamic political identity.
In 1977, Ziaur Rahman removed secularism as a fundamental principle and inserted Bismillah-ar-Rahman-ar-Rahim and a commitment to “absolute trust and faith in Almighty Allah.” In 1988, HM Ershad made Islam the state religion under Article 2A. In 2011, secularism was restored as a fundamental principle, but Bismillah and state religion were retained.
Bangladesh now has a constitution that simultaneously declares the state to be secular and Islam to be the state religion. That legal contradiction is the institutional expression of the identity synthesis described above -- a society that is overwhelmingly Muslim and yet determined that religion should not determine citizenship.
The fascinating historical irony is that Bangladesh’s secularism partly emerged from the failure of Pakistan’s Muslim-nationalist experiment to accommodate Bengali linguistic and cultural nationalism.
It was not an attempt to make Bangladesh less Muslim. It was an attempt to make Bangladesh a state where someone could admire Tagore and Nazrul, celebrate Bengali New Year, and at the same time identify strongly with Islam -- without one identity having to negate the other.
Ziauddin M Choudhury is a former Civil Servant and World Bank Official.

item.title: Why do women entrepreneurs struggle to secure loans?
item.description:
For women entrepreneurs in Bangladesh, getting a bank loan can mean confronting more than interest rates, paperwork, and eligibility requirements. The lending process does not simply involve bank officers and women in the SME sector.
A businesswoman seeking loans may also have to navigate a system shaped by assumptions about who belongs in business, who can handle financial matters, and who deserves to be taken seriously by government officers and other people involved in the lending process.
Although there is growing attention to facilitating women in funding their ventures in this country, gendered attitudes can make the loan application process a difficult and discouraging experience.
The case of guarantors for bank loans can illustrate the difficulty women face in accessing external funds for their small or medium businesses. Generally, loan applications require guarantors who satisfy particular conditions, such as being established businesspeople, government employees, or property owners.
When lending practices favour or expect male guarantors, women entrepreneurs may have difficulty identifying people within their professional and social networks who meet these requirements.
Women have had fewer opportunities to develop relationships with senior businesspeople, property owners, or officials due to their extensive workload at home and work or the patriarchal norms of having a distance from males in society.
Consequently, women entrepreneurs may have a smaller pool of people who can meet the bank's requirements or even struggle to find any of them.
The problem goes beyond the availability of potential guarantors. It can also reflect perceptions about women's credibility as business owners.
Given the gender stereotypical attitude, some potential guarantors may be reluctant to assume responsibility for a woman's business loan. Concerns about the legitimacy, stability, or financial prospects of a woman-owned business can make an already demanding requirement even more difficult to fulfil.
The collateral for bank loans is another powerful example to consider. As women in our society lack property, the collateral issue has received certain attention in the lending process.
While women have flexibility regarding collateral in applying for small amounts of loans, the case is complicated for seeking large loans. The problem is not restricted to simply not possessing property; it can be extended to providing necessary documents in banks to place collateral.
Obtaining these documents can involve interaction with land registration offices and other public institutions. Women may find themselves waiting longer, having difficulty obtaining assistance or feeling that their concerns are not taken as seriously as those of male applicants.
The issue is not necessarily that men receive uniformly favourable treatment. However, gender can add another layer of disadvantage for women when social expectations define business dealings, negotiation, and interaction with public officials as predominantly male activities.
Gender discrimination can take the form of subtle neglect, dismissive behaviour or an assumption that a woman is less capable of handling business-related matters independently.
This creates an additional burden for women seeking finance. A procedure that should be purely administrative can become an uncomfortable social encounter.
When women anticipate such treatment, some may become reluctant to approach public offices independently, thereby making the loan application process more complicated and time-consuming.
In short, when women encounter gender-biased attitudes during these processes, access to finance can become dependent not only on their business credentials but also on their ability to navigate gendered institutional environments.
As a result of such gendered problems, some women may seek smaller loans than they actually require, postpone expansion plans, rely on informal financing or avoid borrowing altogether.
Such outcomes matter not only for individual women entrepreneurs but also for the wider economy. When women-owned businesses cannot obtain adequate finance, opportunities for business expansion, employment creation, and income generation can also be constrained.
Improving women's access to credit therefore requires attention not only to the availability of financial products but also to the conditions under which those products are accessed.
Ensuring that women entrepreneurs can access formal finance requires removing not only the visible barriers written into loan procedures but also the less visible barriers created by social attitudes and institutional practices.
Banks need to design the lending process more critically to address the patriarchal problems associated with it. For instance, requirements concerning guarantors deserve careful consideration. Banks can examine whether particular requirements unintentionally disadvantage women entrepreneurs and whether alternative mechanisms can assess creditworthiness without unnecessarily restricting access to finance.
It is also important to take into account the social and institutional environment surrounding the lending process, which is not directly related to banks.
Public-sector employees need greater awareness of gender-sensitive service delivery. Women applicants should be treated consistently and respectfully, while procedures for documentation and communication should be sufficiently transparent that applicants do not have to depend on informal influence or personal connections.
Women's access to bank loans is not simply a question of whether a loan facility exists. It is also a question of whether women can enter the lending process on equal terms. In a deeply patriarchal society, dismantling the gendered obstacles will not be straightforward. Government agencies and financial institutions therefore need to work together to make lending practices more accessible, transparent, and responsive to women entrepreneurs.
Dr Jasmine Jaim is a Professor at Institute of Business Administration, Jahangirnagar University. She is an Associate Editor of the international journal Gender, Work and Organization, and social entrepreneur in the creative industry. The article has been developed based on the journal article “Bank loans access for women business-owners in Bangladesh: Obstacles and dependence on husbands” published in “Journal of Small Business Management.”

item.title: Envoy: Iran ready to retaliate if US, Israel launch nuclear attack
item.description:
Iran is prepared to respond if the United States or Israel launches a nuclear attack against the country, Iranian Ambassador to Bangladesh Jalil Rahimi Jahanabadi has said, warning that another strike on Iran could take place at any moment.
Speaking at an exchange of views organised by the Iranian Embassy in Dhaka, the ambassador said negotiations mediated by Oman had been moving towards a breakthrough before the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran.
Responding to questions from journalists, he discussed Iran's position on the conflict, its nuclear programme, the Strait of Hormuz and Bangladesh's energy and shipping concerns.
The ambassador said the conflict had been ongoing for nine months and that the US had failed to achieve its objectives.
“The Omani foreign minister announced at night that the negotiations were moving towards success. But the next morning, the US and Israel attacked us. Our understanding is that the US and Israel do not understand the logic. They do not believe in democracy. For them, negotiations mean surrender,” he said.
He claimed that the objectives of the campaign against Iran included changing its political system, bringing opposition groups into the country from neighbouring states, destroying its missile capabilities and removing its uranium from the country.
“None of these objectives has been achieved. All US bases are now within the range of our attacks,” he said.
The ambassador further claimed that more than 450 Iranian civilians, including the country's supreme leader and military commanders, had been killed in the conflict.
He said the war marked the beginning of the end of US global dominance.
Predicting another round of fighting, he said negotiations might not produce a promising outcome, although Iran remained committed to dialogue.
“My prediction is that there will be another war. Negotiations may not be very promising. However, we believe in democracy and dialogue. What America failed to achieve through war, it now wants to secure at the negotiating table. We have prepared ourselves for another war, but we are also continuing honest negotiations through mediators,” he said.
Asked whether the US could launch a nuclear attack against Iran, the ambassador said Washington's past use of nuclear weapons meant such a possibility could not be ruled out.
“The US has a history of using nuclear weapons. So it could commit this crime again. America is now in a difficult position, and its global credibility is at risk. To save itself, it could commit any crime, including a nuclear attack,” he said.
Asked whether Iran considered the US or Israel its bigger adversary, he said Tehran did not distinguish between the two.
“We see no difference between America and Israel. In our view, Israel is a state of America. Israel determines US policy. Zionists control America's economy, security and culture,” he claimed.
Asked how Iran would prevent a nuclear attack, the ambassador said he did not see rationality in the US president's approach and therefore believed such an attack might not be preventable.
“But if such an attack takes place, we will give the US and Israel a strong response,” he said.
On the prospect of reopening the Strait of Hormuz, the ambassador said Iran had discussed the issue with Oman and Qatar but had no immediate plans to restore access.
He said the strait would remain closed until the US lifted its blockade of Iran.
“We have told the US that we are prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if it lifts the blockade, commits not to attack us again and accepts the conditions we have previously announced,” he said.
Asked how Iran would help countries such as Bangladesh, which depend on energy supplies passing through the Strait of Hormuz, if the conflict continued and the waterway remained closed, the ambassador said no country could be assisted in the Persian Gulf until the war ended.
However, he said Bangladeshi vessels could pass through the strait if they met two conditions: coordinating their movements with Iran and following routes designated by Tehran as safe.
“Ships are still moving through the strait every day. Those that come under attack or strike mines are travelling outside the routes designated by us. If they follow the designated routes and inform us, there will be no problem,” he said.
Asked whether any Bangladeshi fuel-carrying vessels had used the route, the ambassador said the information was available to the Bangladesh government.
“We keep records of vessel movements, but we do not want to disclose which country's ships are travelling for what purpose, so that misunderstandings do not arise between countries,” he said.
He added that patrols were still operating in the area and no Bangladeshi vessel had been attacked, which he said demonstrated that the arrangement was working.

item.title: EWU hosts first independently organized TEDx event
item.description:
East West University (EWU) hosted its first independently organized TEDx event, TEDxEWU Bangladesh 2026, at the Manzur Elahi Auditorium on October 31, featuring 8 speakers under the theme “Where We Become”.
The event featured speakers from diverse professional backgrounds, including Rubina Jahan, Dr Anisur Rahman, Amitabh Reza Chowdhury, Nayeem Ashraf, Shwapna Bhowmick, Munia Islam Mozumder, Nusrat Imrose Tisha and Aedid Rashid.
Through their talks, the speakers explored topics including personal growth, perseverance, career transitions, creativity, leadership and overcoming challenges. Their presentations offered students, faculty members and alumni perspectives on personal development, aspirations and future possibilities.
The event also provided a platform for intellectual exchange, encouraging attendees to reflect on their personal journeys and consider new approaches to growth and change.
As part of the program, Dr Farhana Ferdousi, chairperson of EWU's Department of Business Administration, presented crests of appreciation to the speakers in recognition of their contributions.
The inaugural event marked an initiative by EWU to promote curiosity, creativity and the exchange of ideas within its academic community.

item.title: HSC supplementary exams to begin on December 1
item.description:
Supplementary examinations for students who failed in up to two subjects in the 2026 Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) and equivalent examinations will begin on December 1.
Both regular and irregular candidates will be eligible to sit the exams. The detailed schedule will be published later on the websites of the respective education boards.
The information was announced in a press release signed by Bangladesh Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee President and Dhaka Education Board Chairman Professor Syed Anwaruzzaman on Wednesday.
According to the release, students who appeared as regular or irregular candidates in the 2026 HSC and equivalent examinations and failed in a maximum of two subjects will be eligible for the supplementary exams.
Meanwhile, the Dhaka Education Board has published a separate notice outlining the form fill-up schedule for the supplementary examinations.
Online form fill-up will run from November 5 to 9. The deadline for paying examination fees through Sonali Bank's Sonali Seba service is November 10.
According to the Dhaka Board notice, the fee is Tk125 for each theoretical paper or subject and Tk25 for each practical paper or subject. A centre fee of Tk450 will also be charged per candidate.
Supplementary examinations for regular candidates will be held under the full 2026 syllabus, while irregular candidates will sit the exams under the revised 2025 syllabus.

item.title: Tahsif Souri's female friend placed on 3-day remand in murder case
item.description:
A Dhaka court has placed the female friend of former Air Force official Tahsif Souri on a fresh three-day remand in a murder case filed over the recovery of his body.
The order was passed by Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Manzurul Islam on Wednesday afternoon after a hearing, prosecution lawyer Omar Faruk Faruqi confirmed.
The investigation officer, Inspector Firoz Uddin of the Tongi River Police outpost, produced the accused before the court after the end of her four-day remand and sought a fresh seven-day remand.
In the application, the investigation officer said the woman was questioned for four days from November 1 following a court order.
During interrogation, she said she had gone to Nest Bar and Restaurant in Uttara with Souri on the night of October 27, before the incident. She also said they had eaten at a fried chicken shop several times that evening and visited different places, including a motorcycle garage.
The application said the woman had provided several important pieces of information about the case during interrogation. These were kept confidential and verified for the sake of the investigation.
However, the investigation officer said the woman tactfully avoided answering several questions and remained silent during interrogation.
Another suspect in the case, Ahmed Shahriar Reza Dip, is also in police custody on remand. The investigation officer said the statements of the two suspects needed to be cross-checked to identify inconsistencies and similarities.
A review of Souri's mobile phone call records also showed that he had spoken to his female friend several times, the application said.
The investigation officer added that preliminary investigations had found evidence of the woman's involvement in the murder.
In the fresh remand application, the investigation officer cited seven reasons for further interrogation.
These included determining whether Souri and the woman had any arguments or altercations at the fried chicken shop and Nest Bar and Restaurant in Sector 18 of Uttara on the day of the incident, and whether there had been any tension in their relationship before the incident.
The investigation officer also said further interrogation was necessary to uncover the motive behind the murder, identify and arrest other suspects, recover evidence and cross-check the statements of the two accused.
The defence lawyers, including Mohammad Iman Hossain and Abdur Rahman, sought cancellation of the remand and bail for the accused. The prosecution opposed the plea.
After hearing both sides, the court granted a three-day remand.
The woman was detained from the Kafrul area around 2am on October 31. The following day, the court granted her a four-day remand.
Dip was also placed on a three-day remand in a separate order in connection with the same case.
Souri went missing after leaving home on the evening of October 27 at the invitation of his junior friend Dip.
His body was recovered by river police from the Rajabari Ghat area of the Turag River the following afternoon.
Souri's father, KM Enayetul Karim, filed a murder case against unidentified persons with Uttarkhan police station at 1:05am on October 30.

item.title: Sajek blockade chokes supplies, paralyses local economy
item.description:
Sajek in Rangamati has remained under a blockade for 14 consecutive days, disrupting road communication, triggering shortages of essential commodities and bringing tourism-related businesses to a standstill.
No vehicles operated on the Sajek road on Wednesday, leaving residents struggling to access food and other daily necessities. Farmers are also unable to transport their produce to markets, putting their livelihoods at risk.
Hundreds of drivers and their assistants who depend on transporting tourists have lost their income. Many are borrowing money to support their families, while vehicle owners who purchased vehicles with loans are struggling to repay instalments.
Meanwhile, the Parbatya Chattagram Rakkha Committee has announced a separate 48-hour blockade for November 4 and 5, protesting the ongoing blockade in Sajek. The program was announced in a press release signed by the organization's member secretary, Bindu Lal Chakma, on Tuesday evening.
The move has further complicated efforts to resolve the crisis through dialogue between the administration and protesters.
Although progress was made on four of the five demands raised by the protesters, no agreement has been reached on the main point of contention. At a meeting between protesters and a government delegation in Ujobaazar on October 26, the two sides reached an understanding on four demands. However, disagreements over the demand to remove armed JSS members from Sajek prevented a final agreement.
The Sajek Gono Odhikar Rakkha Committee and Sajek Karbari Association resumed the blockade on Monday, November 2, after a one-day relaxation on November 1. On Tuesday, protesters placed tree trunks and lit fires at several points along the Sajek tourist road, effectively halting traffic.
However, leaders of the two organizations have announced exemptions for vehicles carrying locally produced agricultural goods, teachers, and students.
In a joint statement on Tuesday, Sajek Gono Odhikar Rakkha Committee convener Babudhan Chakma and Sajek Karbari Association president Natun Joy Chakma said the decision was taken at a joint meeting of the organizations.
Vehicles carrying agricultural produce and transporting teachers and students to educational institutions will be exempt from the blockade. Earlier exemptions for ambulances, electricity supply vehicles, vehicles used for religious and wedding ceremonies, and journalists' vehicles will also remain in place.
The leaders said the decision was taken considering the interests of farmers and agricultural traders from both the Pahari and Bengali communities. However, they reiterated that the blockade would continue until all five demands were met.
Baghaichhari Upazila Nirbahi Officer Amena Marjan said no decision had been made on holding another meeting. She added that Sajek Valley would remain closed until further notice on the instructions of the district administration due to security concerns.
On November 1, protesters announced a 12-hour relaxation to allow residents to collect food and other essential supplies. However, a counter-blockade by the Parbatya Chattagram Rakkha Committee and a work abstention by transport owners and workers prevented normal traffic from resuming.
Rahul Chakma, organizing secretary of the Sajek Resort-Cottage Owners Association, said the tourism-dependent economy had been hit hardest by the crisis.
With no tourists, resorts, cottages, restaurants, transport services, local shops and other tourism-related businesses have virtually ground to a halt.
He estimated that the blockade had already caused losses of Tk30-35 crore, warning that the figure could rise further if the disruption continued.
According to him, Sajek has more than 116 resorts, 14 restaurants and over 100 small and large shops. The prolonged absence of tourists has left business owners, cottage operators and employees struggling to make ends meet.
The blockade has also disrupted road communication between Sajek, Baghaichhari upazila headquarters and Khagrachhari, worsening shortages of rice, lentils and other essential commodities.
Anitya Tripura, a member of Ward 2 of Sajek Union Parishad, said residents were running out of food and other essential supplies stored at home. Five shops in Ruilui Para had also run out of daily necessities.
Jaupeithang Tripura, headman of Shialdai Mouza and a union parishad member, said farmers and small traders were unable to take their produce to markets because of the blockade and the absence of tourists. He said the disruption had paralyzed the rural economy, with shortages of medicines and other essential goods also emerging.
Khagrachhari Transport Owners' Association president Ayush Chakma said the association had 250 registered vehicles, while the Jeep Owners' Association had more than 500. In addition, more than 1,500 vehicles, including Mahindra three-wheelers, Chander Gari and CNG-run auto-rickshaws, operate in Sajek.
He said the blockade had cut off the income of drivers and their assistants, while many vehicle owners were struggling to repay loans. The transport sector in the district was suffering estimated daily losses of Tk30-40 lakh, he added.
Sajek police station Officer-in-Charge Tofazzal Hossain said large vehicles were not operating on the road due to the blockade, although a few auto-rickshaws and motorcycles were moving occasionally.
He said the situation remained calm and peaceful, with no major untoward incidents reported so far.
The latest blockade began on October 22, following earlier disruptions. A temporary relaxation was announced from October 16 to 21 for Durga Puja, while tourism activities had already been suspended following a blockade that began on October 11.
Despite repeated blockades and temporary relaxations, no lasting solution has emerged, leaving residents, farmers, businesses and transport workers uncertain about when normal life will resume.
