item.title: Clashes during garment protests leave 50 injured, 200 factories shut
item.description:
Garment workers continued protests across several industrial areas on Wednesday, demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000, as clashes with police left at least 50 people injured, including law enforcement personnel, and forced more than 200 factories in Savar and Ashulia to declare holidays.
Demonstrations, road blockades and confrontations were reported in Savar, Ashulia, Gazipur and Narayanganj, while additional security forces were deployed in several areas to contain the unrest.
In Savar, clashes broke out in the Padma Mor area of Hemayetpur around 8:15am and later spread to Ulail, where workers confronted police in front of the Al-Muslim Group factory around 9am.
Workers threw bricks and stones at police, who responded with tear gas shells, sound grenades and rubber bullets. A police vehicle belonging to the officer-in-charge of Savar Model Police Station was also set on fire.
Dhaka District Superintendent of Police Shamima Parveen said at least 50 people, including police personnel, workers and passersby, were injured. OC Saiful Alam sustained serious injuries, she added.
The confrontation began after workers gathered near Padma Mor to press their wage demands. Police attempted to clear the road after protesters occupied it, triggering clashes that later spread to nearby locations.
Around 9:10am, workers blocked the Dhaka-Aricha highway, bringing traffic in both directions to a halt and causing severe congestion. Between 30,000 and 40,000 workers had gathered in the area from both directions, Shamima said.
Several factories in Hemayetpur, Ulail and surrounding areas later declared holidays amid the unrest, with some workers returning home peacefully.
Three platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) personnel were deployed in Savar and Ashulia to strengthen security in the industrial belt.
Meanwhile, garment workers in Gazipur blocked the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway near Signboard in the Gacha area around 9:30am, bringing traffic to a standstill.
Between 2,000 and 4,000 workers took to the streets, throwing bricks and stones at police during a standoff. Law enforcement personnel fired tear gas shells and sound grenades to disperse them.
Mohammad Amjad Hossain, superintendent of Gazipur Industrial Police, said another group of workers had gathered near Joydebpur around 8:30am but was dispersed. He said the situation remained stable in Salna, Rajendrapur, Shafipur and Palli Bidyut, while tension persisted near Kashimpur.
In Narayanganj, garment workers from several factories in Fatullah took to the streets for the third consecutive day. Tensions escalated around 10:30am near Katherpul in Kutubail, adjacent to the Dhaka-Narayanganj Link Road, when workers attempted to block the road.
Police fired tear gas shells and sound grenades to disperse the protesters following chases and counter-chases. Five people were detained.
Workers said they had been demonstrating peacefully when BNP leaders arrived and assaulted some of them, prompting police intervention. Local shopkeeper Jamal Mia, however, said an argument had broken out between workers and local BNP activists before police arrived.
Additional Superintendent of Police Tarek Al Mehedi said five people had been detained in connection with the incident.
In the capital, police increased security in Mirpur and Uttara as protests continued. Police dispersed workers gathered outside several factories in Pallabi and near Purabi Cinema Hall in Mirpur-11, although no major incidents were reported.
In Uttara, police and other law enforcement personnel took positions along the stretch from Rajlokkhi to the airport, with water cannons and police vans stationed in the area.
Md Hafizur Rahman, officer-in-charge of Mirpur Model Police Station, said seven of the eight garment factories under his jurisdiction remained operational. Workers at one factory had briefly stopped working but resumed after being persuaded to do so.
By Wednesday evening, more than 200 garment factories in Savar and Ashulia had declared holidays amid concerns over workers' safety and the deteriorating situation in the industrial areas.
Industrial Police-1 Superintendent of Police Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan confirmed the closures.
Shamima Parveen alleged that unidentified troublemakers were exploiting the workers' presence to create instability. She said police had detained one person in Hemayetpur with a crude bomb and another over the torching of a police vehicle.
BGB headquarters public relations officer Shariful Islam said a total of 24 platoons had been deployed across key industrial areas in Savar-Ashulia, Gazipur and Narayanganj to maintain security and prevent further incidents.
Of these, five platoons were deployed in Hemayetpur, Ashulia and Baipail; 13 in different parts of Gazipur, including Chowrasta, Bhogra Bypass, Chandra and Kaliakair; and six in Narayanganj.
The workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000, saying the current minimum wage of Tk12,500 is insufficient to meet the rising cost of living.
Their five-point demands also include introducing rationing facilities in all garment factories, ensuring the right to form trade unions, ending arbitrary dismissals and blacklisting, and ensuring justice over the deaths of workers, including Amjad Hossain Kamal.
They have also called for the full implementation of labour laws.
The unrest has continued since Monday, with workers staging demonstrations and blocking roads in Mirpur, Gazipur, Savar, Ashulia and Narayanganj. Tuesday's protests also resulted in clashes and running battles with police, leaving around 10 police officers injured and four workers detained.
Meanwhile, garment worker Taufiq Sheikh, 22, who was injured during unrest in Gazipur on Monday, died while undergoing treatment at Shin Shin Japan Hospital in Uttara on Tuesday afternoon.
A junior layman in the cutting section of Laila Styles Ltd, Taufiq was reportedly recording the unrest on his mobile phone when he was attacked and beaten, according to his family. His body was taken to his village in Chhaygharia, Gobindaganj, Gaibandha, on Tuesday night. His janaza was scheduled for yesterday morning.
The protests have disrupted production at several factories and forced some to suspend operations as tensions persist across the country's major garment-producing areas.

item.title: Journalists seek Iqbal Sobhan, Rajib Ghosh's release; clarity over DB questioning
item.description:
Journalists and social media users have expressed concern over former information adviser Iqbal Sobhan Chowdhury and DBC News Crime Chief Rajib Ghosh being taken to the Detective Branch (DB) office, with several professional bodies calling for clarification and Rajib’s release.
On Wednesday afternoon, DB officials took the two from the DBC News office in Mohakhali to the DB office on Minto Road in Dhaka. They are being questioned by the police.
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said that if Iqbal had been detained, there must be specific allegations against him. He added that the matter would be examined in accordance with the law.
DMP Deputy Commissioner (Media) Md Akhtar Hossain said an unwanted situation had developed at the DBC office over the broadcast of a news report.
He said the two were taken to the DB office for their safety and questioning. Neither had been detained or arrested, he added, saying a decision would be made after the questioning.
Journalist Muktadir Rashid Romeo expressed concern in a Facebook post, calling for Rajib to be returned respectfully to his workplace.
He said taking a journalist into DB custody without specific allegations was alarming and amounted to an attack on journalism.
The Journalists Against Repression Front condemned the incident involving Iqbal and demanded his release. In a statement, the organisation’s Convener Akhtar Hossain and Member Secretary Sheikh Jamal voiced concern over the incident.
Iqbal is a former president of the Bangladesh Federal Union of Journalists (BFUJ), editor of The Daily Observer and former chairman of DBC News. He also served as information adviser to former prime minister Sheikh Hasina.
The Association of Television News Broadcasters (ATJFB) also expressed concern over the incident. In a joint statement, its President Tanzim Anwar and General Secretary Baten Biplob said there was no clarity about whether an arrest warrant had been issued or what legal process had been followed.
They called for due process, transparency and respect for the rights of those involved, and urged the authorities to release Rajib immediately.
The Dhaka Reporters Unity (DRU) also expressed concern, with its President Abu Saleh Akon and General Secretary Mynul Hasan Sohel demanding that the authorities disclose the whereabouts of the two to their families and colleagues.
The organisation called for their release if there was no legal basis for holding them.

item.title: Trump weakened at home, Iran threatens wider war
item.description:
Iran’s supreme leader warned on Wednesday that the Middle East war would widen if the US resumes its attacks, dismissing hopes of a policy shift in Washington after midterm elections dealt a blow to President Donald Trump.
Trump has recently threatened to renew the war against Iran amid similar rhetoric from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, but on Tuesday he suffered a resounding defeat in polls that will strip his Republicans of control over Congress.
The results could constrain Trump’s ability to enact his agenda, though the president retains the power to order new strikes.
“Those who still harbour even the slightest hope that the behaviour of the hegemonic system might change through partisan or factional shifts, or who imagine that making concessions to the United States can dissuade it from hostility towards the Iranian nation, are seriously mistaken,” Iranian supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei said in a written statement Wednesday.
He also warned that if the United States did choose further military action, the scope of the war would widen, without elaborating.
Khamenei has yet to appear in public since he took power in March following the killing of his father and predecessor in US-Israeli strikes, and has communicated through written messages.
Earlier, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s chief negotiator in talks with the US, said Americans had voted against war in the midterms.
“Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” he posted on X.
“If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare,” Ghalibaf said.
Iran’s judiciary chief Gholamhossein Mohseni Ejei also hailed the election results, saying Trump had been “defeated both militarily and politically”.
The war has proved unpopular among the US public, who have seen the cost of living rise after a spike in energy prices caused by the war.
Trump on Tuesday acknowledged the conflict may have played a part in the defeat of his Republican Party.
“I think a part of it was Iran, but at the same time, people understood the importance of what I’ve done,” Trump told Fox News.
On Tuesday the US launched strikes on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, with Iranian state media reporting five explosions in rapid succession.
“They built an anti-aircraft facility... As soon as it was completed, we hit it last night very nicely,” Trump told US media, but he called it a “minor attack”.
Earlier this week the president said he still had to “take care” of one or two targets, including so-called Pickaxe Mountain in central Iran, a suspected nuclear site which Tehran denies is such a facility.
However, he told the Financial Times newspaper on Tuesday that a full-scale resumption of war may not be necessary.
“We seem to be getting everything we want,” he said. “I’m ready, we’re ready. We’re locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no reason for it.”
The president’s remarks come with diplomatic efforts by mediators in full swing in an attempt to prevent any resumption of fighting.
On Tuesday Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said his government was still trying to resolve the crisis through dialogue.
Pezeshkian said Iran’s supreme leader had granted the government new powers to negotiate on issues previously off-limits.
Qatar, a mediator in the protracted wrangling, said it remained hopeful of an interim deal.
Both sides “are currently reviewing the ideas and proposals we have presented”, Qatari foreign ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari told reporters.
China also said Wednesday that avoiding a return to hostilities was a top priority in its diplomatic efforts with the countries.
The war, triggered in February when the US and Israel pummelled Iran in a massive wave of strikes, has been at a stalemate for months.
Iranian officials have repeatedly warned of wide-ranging retaliation if Washington resumes the war.

item.title: Speakers call for legal reforms, accountability to uphold constitutional rights
item.description:
Constitutional guarantees of fundamental rights must be backed by effective legal safeguards and accountable state institutions to ensure their protection in practice, speakers said at a Constitution Day discussion held at the Supreme Court Bar Association auditorium on Wednesday.
They called for legal reforms and stronger institutional accountability to ensure the effective implementation of rights, including equality, personal liberty, freedom of expression and the right to life.
The discussion, titled “54 Years of the Constitution: Rights and Protection Achievements and Realities,” was jointly organized by the Bangladesh Legal Aid and Services Trust (BLAST), the Supreme Court Lawyers Guild and Banglar Pathshala Foundation.
Senior Supreme Court lawyer and BLAST Honorary Executive Director Sara Hossain moderated the discussion. Acknowledging the Constitution's achievements, she stressed the need to address gaps in its implementation.
In his welcome address, Ahmed Javed, assistant professor of economics at City University and founder of Banglar Pathshala Foundation, questioned whether ordinary citizens had equal access to the justice system compared to powerful individuals. He also raised concerns about people who remained outside the protection of constitutional safeguards.
Discussing equality, Nurunnahar Urmi, lecturer in the Department of Law and Justice at Presidency University, said fulfilling the constitutional promise of equality required consideration of people's different social positions and lived experiences.
She emphasized the need to move beyond formal equality and ensure substantive equality for women, Indigenous communities and other disadvantaged groups.
Addressing arrest, detention and personal liberty, Supreme Court lawyer MM Khalequzzaman highlighted the experiences of people subjected to arrest and custodial torture. He stressed the need for effective enforcement of constitutional safeguards and legal reforms to protect individual liberty.
Supreme Court lawyer Priya Ahsan Chowdhury said existing laws, including those inherited from the colonial period, needed to be reviewed and reformed to align with the right to freedom of expression.
She stressed that laws must not be used to suppress dissent and called for any restrictions on freedom of expression to comply with the principles of necessity and proportionality under international human rights standards.
Environment rights activist and researcher Barish Hasan Chowdhury highlighted the connection between environmental protection and the right to life.
He stressed the need to implement constitutional commitments on environmental protection while considering the rights of marginalized communities and the interests of present and future generations in addressing the impacts of climate change.
In his concluding remarks, senior Supreme Court lawyer Prabir Niyogi described the 1972 Constitution as highly progressive for its time.
He said the main challenge to protecting constitutional rights lay in shortcomings in their implementation.
Niyogi said decisions on constitutional amendments should be based on an understanding of the Constitution's historical background and thorough research. He added that amendments must follow the procedures prescribed by the Constitution while it remains in force.
He also underscored the Supreme Court's role as the guardian and interpreter of the Constitution.
Retired Appellate Division judge Borhan Uddin described the Constitution as a commitment by the state to its people on how the country would be governed.
He said the Constitution's survival despite numerous amendments was an achievement, but its implementation required regular review.
Questioning the effectiveness of safeguards against torture despite its prohibition, he said arrest or imprisonment did not deprive anyone of their human dignity.
He also stressed the judiciary's responsibility to protect the fundamental rights of all citizens, including workers, young people and women.
In his vote of thanks, Khandaker Shahriar Shakir said the Constitution defined the relationship between individuals and the state, while protecting citizens' rights remained a state responsibility.
He called on the government to establish an effective mechanism to implement Supreme Court directives and judgments.
Shakir also stressed that no one should face legal cases or arrest simply for criticizing the government.
He urged stakeholders to assess whether reform initiatives were making meaningful progress in reflecting the aspirations expressed by the people during the July 2024 uprising.

item.title: Three organizers detained while putting up posters in Chittagong
item.description:
Three organizers of the Revolutionary Workers Movement and the Revolutionary Student-Youth Movement were detained by police while putting up posters supporting the garment workers' movement in the Chittagong Export Processing Zone (EPZ) area on Wednesday.
The detainees were identified as Rakib Uddin, president of the Chittagong Metropolitan branch of the Revolutionary Workers Movement; Zahid, vice-president of the Chittagong Metropolitan branch of the Revolutionary Student-Youth Movement; and Shanto, a member of the organization.
According to a statement sent by Naim Uddin, vice-president of the National Committee of the Revolutionary Student-Youth Movement, leaders and activists of the 2 organizations were putting up handwritten posters in the EPZ area as part of a campaign supporting the garment workers' movement.
At around 5pm, a police officer grabbed one of the organizers by the hand. All 3 were subsequently taken to a nearby police box for questioning, the statement said.
EPZ police van later arrived to take them to the police station, where they remain detained, according to the statement.
The organization demanded the immediate and unconditional release of the 3 organizers, the release of all individuals arrested in connection with the garment workers' movement, and fulfillment of the workers' legitimate demands.

item.title: US midterm voters deliver brutal verdict on Trump
item.description:
Donald Trump faced a radically transformed and hostile political landscape on Wednesday after US voters handed control of Congress to the Democrats in a stunning rebuke to his presidency.
The result was a personal humiliation for the 80-year-old Trump as a Democratic wave swept into his Republican heartland, boosted by anger at soaring energy costs and his costly, dragging war with Iran.
The Democratic capture of both the Senate and the House of Representatives signals an end to Trump’s stranglehold on US politics and gives Democrats the power to block legislation, launch investigations into Trump’s administration and thwart his appointments.
The results reflected deep frustration over the cost of living, tariffs and Trump’s war with Iran, which has sent fuel prices soaring and compounded dissatisfaction with an already deeply unpopular president.
“This is so incredibly exciting. We can get our country back,” Kathy Jackoway said in Texas, celebrating a win by Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico.
Trump struck a conciliatory tone despite his history of rejecting election defeats, telling The New York Times he was “absolutely willing” to accept the results.
“I think the Democrats did a good job,” the 80-year-old told Fox News, in rare praise for his political opponents. “They fought hard.”
But he sought to distance himself from his party’s poor showing, adding: “I don’t view it as a hit on me.”
He acknowledged that the Iran conflict had contributed to the result but defended the military campaign, and he suggested the rival parties could find common ground on immigration.
Republican heartland
Democrats flipped seats that had long been held by Republicans, scoring breakthroughs in South Carolina, North Carolina, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Texas and Maine.
In Maine, former logger Troy Jackson defeated longtime Republican Senator Susan Collins.
In Kansas, Methodist minister Adam Hamilton became the first Democrat elected to the Senate from the reliably conservative state since 1932.
Iowa had not elected a Democratic senator since 2008.
In Texas, Democrats won not only a Senate seat but also the governor’s race, ending decades of Republican rule.
Democrats protected key Senate seats of their own, including Jon Ossoff in Georgia and an open seat in New Hampshire.
In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed defeated former Republican lawmaker Mike Rogers, making him the first Muslim elected to the upper chamber of Congress.
El-Sayed won despite a last-minute curveball when congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary to El-Sayed, came out in support of Rogers.
In the House, Democrats made gains in Pennsylvania, Kentucky, Arizona, North Carolina, Wisconsin and New Jersey, including districts Trump had carried comfortably in 2024.
Democrats also won Georgia’s governorship, electing former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms as the first Black woman governor in US history.
Republicans had some consolation in Florida, where Trump-backed Byron Donalds became the state’s first Black governor and Ashley Moody retained a Senate seat.
But the night was “a big wipeout and a strong repudiation of Donald Trump and his policies,” George Washington University professor Todd Belt told AFP.
Trump on defensive
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries declared Trump’s MAGA movement “on the run.”
Jeffries could become the first Black speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes in January.
Trump insisted on social media that Republicans would have won “IN A LANDSLIDE” if he had been running, though he had repeatedly urged supporters throughout the campaign to “pretend I’m on the ballot.”
He also repeated his threat to use the presidential veto on Democrat-passed bills, posting a picture on social media of a red baseball cap reading just: “VETO.”
On the international front, Russia said it hoped Trump will continue his “peacemaking efforts” and China said it would “continue working” with the United States.
Iran’s supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei said he did not expect the election results to bring about a shift in US policy.
